Question 9 (i) : la serie geometrique converge pour |x/(2x-1)| < 1 ; la valeur x = -3 donne r = 3/7, condition verifiee.

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\left(\dfrac{x}{2x-1}\right) + \left(\dfrac{x}{2x-1}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{x}{2x-1}\right)^3 + \cdots = \dfrac34$, find the value of $x$. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The series is geometric with first term $r$ and common ratio $r$, where $r = \dfrac{x}{2x-1}$. For a convergent geometric series ($|r| < 1$) the sum to infinity is $\dfrac{a}{1 - r}$ with $a = r$:

$$\frac{r}{1 - r} = \frac34 \Longrightarrow 4r = 3(1 - r) \Longrightarrow 7r = 3 \Longrightarrow r = \frac37.$$

Now solve $\dfrac{x}{2x - 1} = \dfrac37$:

$$7x = 3(2x - 1) = 6x - 3 \Longrightarrow x = -3.$$

Check: $r = \dfrac{-3}{2(-3) - 1} = \dfrac{-3}{-7} = \dfrac37$, and $|r| = \dfrac37 < 1$, so the series converges. The sum is $\dfrac{3/7}{4/7} = \dfrac34$. Correct.

$$\boxed{x = -3}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: A linear transformation $T$ is represented by the matrix $\mathbf{A}$, where $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&5\\3&5&6\end{pmatrix}$. Find the image of the point $(-5, 2, 1)$ under $T$. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The image of the point with position vector $(x, y, z)^T$ is $\mathbf{A}(x, y, z)^T$:

$$\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&5\\3&5&6\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-5\\2\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1(-5) + 2(2) + 3(1)\\ 2(-5) + 4(2) + 5(1)\\ 3(-5) + 5(2) + 6(1)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-5 + 4 + 3\\ -10 + 8 + 5\\ -15 + 10 + 6\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$

$$\boxed{\text{The image is the point } (2, 3, 1).}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&5\\3&5&6\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix}1&-3&2\\-3&3&-1\\2&-1&0\end{pmatrix}$, find the matrix product $\mathbf{BA}$. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Row by column multiplication:

Row 1 of $\mathbf{B}$ $= (1, -3, 2)$: $\ 1 - 6 + 6 = 1,\quad 2 - 12 + 10 = 0,\quad 3 - 15 + 12 = 0$.

Row 2 of $\mathbf{B}$ $= (-3, 3, -1)$: $\ -3 + 6 - 3 = 0,\quad -6 + 12 - 5 = 1,\quad -9 + 15 - 6 = 0$.

Row 3 of $\mathbf{B}$ $= (2, -1, 0)$: $\ 2 - 2 + 0 = 0,\quad 4 - 4 + 0 = 0,\quad 6 - 5 + 0 = 1$.

$$\mathbf{BA} = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{I}.$$

Hence $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&5\\3&5&6\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix}1&-3&2\\-3&3&-1\\2&-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfy $\mathbf{BA} = \mathbf{I}$, hence or otherwise find the point where the three planes with equations
$$x + 2y + 3z = 5, \qquad 2x + 4y + 5z = 9, \qquad 3x + 4y + 6z = 12$$
intersect. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method 1 - solve the system as printed, by elimination.**

$$
x + 2y + 3z = 5 \tag{1}
$$
$$
2x + 4y + 5z = 9 \tag{2}
$$
$$
3x + 4y + 6z = 12 \tag{3}
$$

$(2) - 2\times(1)$: $(2x + 4y + 5z) - (2x + 4y + 6z) = 9 - 10$, so $-z = -1$ and $z = 1$.

Substitute $z = 1$ into (1): $x + 2y = 2$. Substitute into (3): $3x + 4y = 6$. From $x + 2y = 2$, $x = 2 - 2y$, so $3(2 - 2y) + 4y = 6$, i.e. $6 - 2y = 6$, $y = 0$, then $x = 2$.

The coefficient matrix has determinant $1(24 - 20) - 2(12 - 15) + 3(8 - 12) = 4 + 6 - 12 = -2 \ne 0$, so the three planes meet in exactly one point.

**Method 2 - use $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}$ (the "hence" route).** The first two equations are the first two rows of $\mathbf{A}(x, y, z)^T = (5, 9, 12)^T$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is the matrix of the previous parts (its third row gives $3x + 5y + 6z$). Multiplying by $\mathbf{B}$ on the left:

$$\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{B}\begin{pmatrix}5\\9\\12\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}5 - 27 + 24\\ -15 + 27 - 12\\ 10 - 9 + 0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Both routes give the same point because $y = 0$, so the coefficient of $y$ in the third equation does not affect the solution.

**Check in the printed equations:** (1) $2 + 0 + 3 = 5$; (2) $4 + 0 + 5 = 9$; (3) $6 + 0 + 6 = 12$. All hold.

$$\boxed{\text{The planes intersect at the point } (2, 0, 1).}$$
